61.quote_or_event: “That family, whose son has no spiritual wisdom or contemplation - why didn’t his mother just become a widow? That man who has not practiced devotional worship of the Lord - why didn’t such a sinful man die at birth?”
61.explanation: Bhagat Kabir puts the point in its harshest negative form: a son is worth having only if he has spiritual wisdom; without it, his birth brings his family nothing.
61.tie_back: Kabir says from the other side what Valluvar says positively: the true gain in children lies in their knowing what is worth knowing, not in simply having them.
61.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 328, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
61._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit stated in reverse: both make wisdom the measure of a child's worth, but Kabir means devotional wisdom of God, and his tone is condemnatory where the Kural's is celebratory.

62.quote_or_event: “Those, within whose minds the Lord abides, are robed with honor in the Court of the Lord. They are carried across, along with all their family, and the whole world is saved along with them.”
62.explanation: Guru Ram Das teaches that one person in whom God dwells brings blessing beyond themselves, carrying their whole family across the world-ocean with them.
62.tie_back: Like Valluvar's virtuous child whose good character keeps evil away from the family through seven births, the God-filled person here becomes the means of the family's release.
62.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 310, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
62._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the idea of one person's virtue protecting the whole family matches, but the verse is not about children specifically, and Sikhism ties release to God's grace rather than to transferred merit across seven births.

63.quote_or_event: “His sons did not obey His Word; they turned their backs on Him as Guru... Whatever the Guru said, Lehna did, and so he was installed on the throne.”
63.explanation: The bards Satta and Balwand explain why Guru Nanak passed the Guruship to his disciple Lehna (Guru Angad) and not to his own sons: the inheritance went to the one whose deeds proved him worthy.
63.tie_back: It sharply illustrates the second half of the Kural: whatever wealth the next generation receives comes through each one's own deeds, not by birth.
63.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Pauri 2, Rai Balwand and Satta Doom (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
63._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial and in tension with the first half of the Kural: it confirms that desert follows one's own deeds, but it shows sons who were not their father's true wealth.

64.quote_or_event: “As many mistakes as the son commits, his mother does not hold them against him in her mind.” … “If the son, in anger, runs away, even then, his mother does not hold it against him in her mind.”
64.explanation: Kabir uses a parent's indulgent love, which overlooks whatever mess or mischief a child makes, as the image for God's forgiveness of the devotee.
64.tie_back: It reflects the same parental tenderness the Kural celebrates, in which food a child has messed with becomes sweeter than nectar instead of spoiled.
64.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 478, Raag Asa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
64._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shares the theme of a parent's fond tolerance of a child's mess and mistakes, but it lacks the Kural's image of food and taste and is really a metaphor for God's grace.

65.quote_or_event: “The mind of the poor child is so fickle that he even touches snakes and fire. His mother and father hug him close in their embrace, and so he plays in joy and bliss.”
65.explanation: Guru Arjan draws on the parent's embrace of a small child as a picture of how God holds and protects the devotee.
65.tie_back: Like the Kural's delight in touching one's children, the verse makes the parents' embrace the centre of the image, a moment of shared joy.
65.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1266, Raag Malaar, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
65._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shares the bodily closeness of parent and child, but it does not speak of hearing the child, and the image serves as a metaphor for God's care rather than a statement about parental joy.

66.quote_or_event: “As the child places so much faith in his father, I speak as it pleases the Guru to have me speak.”
66.explanation: In a hymn celebrating the birth of his son, Guru Arjan likens his own speech before the Guru to a small child talking with complete trust to its father.
66.tie_back: Both texts linger on the voice of a child before a loving parent, though only the Kural ranks that voice above the finest music.
66.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 396, Raag Asa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
66._accuracy_note: Next-best only: no SGGS passage was found comparing a child's lisping speech with music; this verse shares only the image of a trusting child speaking to a parent.

67.quote_or_event: Sikh tradition credits Guru Angad, the second Guru, with standardizing the Gurmukhi script and setting up schools to teach the young to read and write in their own Punjabi language rather than in classical Sanskrit.
67.explanation: Britannica reports these traditional attributions, which are central to Sikh memory of Guru Angad, while noting that historical documentation for some of his attributed institutions is limited.
67.tie_back: The Kural says the best thing a father can give his son is learning that wins him a place in the assembly of the wise; Sikh tradition remembers its second Guru as the one who opened learning to the community's children.
67._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shares the priority of educating the young, but it is a Guru's work for a whole community rather than a father's duty to his own son, and Britannica treats the schools as tradition rather than documented history.

68.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
68.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that knowledge truly reflected upon does not stay private; it turns its owner into someone who does good for others.
68.tie_back: Like Valluvar's claim that a child's wisdom delights every living being on earth, the Guru treats knowledge as a good that spreads outward to benefit others.
68.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
68._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shares the idea that wisdom is a public good, but it says nothing of children surpassing their parents, which is the heart of Kural 68.

69.quote_or_event: “O son, this is your mother’s hope and prayer, that you may never forget the Lord, Har, Har, even for an instant. May you ever vibrate upon the Lord of the Universe.”
69.explanation: In this hymn, known among Sikhs as 'Poota Mata Ki Asees' (a mother's blessing to her son), Guru Arjan puts into a mother's mouth her deepest wish: not wealth or rank for her son, but a life of constant remembrance of God.
69.tie_back: Like Valluvar's mother, whose greatest joy is to hear her son called a person of true worth, this mother's highest hope is fixed on her son's character, not on his birth or fortune.
69.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 496, Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
69._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both centre a mother's joy on her son's goodness, but this is a hope and prayer, not the joy of hearing others praise him, and the goodness meant is devotion to God.

70.quote_or_event: “Blessed, blessed is the father; blessed, blessed is the family; blessed, blessed is the mother, who gave birth to the Guru.”
70.explanation: Guru Ram Das praises the True Guru by calling his father, family and mother blessed for having produced him; the child's greatness reflects back on the parents.
70.tie_back: This is almost exactly the response Valluvar says a worthy son should draw from people: seeing him, they call his father blessed.
70.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 310, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
70._accuracy_note: Strong structural fit (a son's worth makes people bless his father), though the son here is the Guru himself, and there is no Kural-style talk of the father's penance.
